Ok boys, my time to shine.
First off though, like /u/calzone said, play through vanilla first. With all the graphics settings on their highest, the game is actually really pretty.

But anyway, lets get to the mods!

FOMM - Fallout Mod Manager. This is pretty much a necessity.
CONELRAD Radio System - Because when Butcher Pete is the Johnny Guitar of FO3, things can get a little annoying.
FO3 Wanderers Edition - Prepare to get your ass kicked by this mod.
Marts Mutant Mod - Probably my favorite mod. It adds a bunch of new enemies and makes their AI like 100x better. The enemies will even fight and loot each other.
Project Beauty - Makes the NPC's less blocky, more pretty.
Fellout - Gets rid of the nasty green tint that you'll eventually learn to hate.
Enhanced Weather - Radioactive snowstorms? Check. Thunder storms that'll make you shit your pants? Check. Weather in general? Double check.
Cube Experiment Mod - You want half life in fallout? Of course you do.
RobCo Certified - When you play through the game, I'm sure you'll notice all the broken down robots all over the place. Well this mod lets you fix em up and use them to your advantage.
High Res Weapons - Just get this one. Trust me.
Alton, IL - Probably the biggest mod I've ever had the pleasure of playing through. It drops you in Alton Illinois with a ton of new stuff to do. Really great mod.
DC Interiors - Makes all those thousands of doors that were previously inaccessible, accessible.

So that's about it for me. If this is your first time modding a game, PLEASE read everything on all of the mods pages. Some mods may or may not conflict with others, and some of them need other mods to run correctly.
Other than that, have fun!

The best mod I can recommend is actually buying Fallout: NV ultimate edition and then downloading TTW (Tale of Two Wastelands). Also buy Fallout 3 GOTY edition if you didn't already. TTW will still allow you to experience Fallout 3 in its entirety but with the added benefits of more weapons, weapon mods, and improve gunplay from Fallout: NV.

I've dabbled and have been actively addicted to a number of things in my life. I've gotten hooked on pain pills (vicodin), have been a pothead, have gambled, have had a porn addiction - I also used to drink everyday (although I was pretty regimented about it.... although it WAS every day... m'eh who knows). Anyways, so I had my fingers in a number of different things.

But my main thing was porn. Porn, lots of it, for hours at a time, and frequently the worst kind - teen and underaged porn, hardcore, heck - there was a time where I'd watch snuff films on the web for thrills (although that wasn't exactly sexual - just compulsive). It was almost as if I just had to lower myself as far as I could go.

So, I guess I would say that porn is / was my "drug of choice," only because it really sent me into the most destructive of places - not to say that the pills didn't send me downhill pretty fast. The pot was definitely financially ruining, at least somewhat - I spent tons of money on that stuff over the years, as I did the booze. But porn - that really was something that almost killed my soul. I definitely have a problem with gambling, one could say I was addicted to it - but it was almost a sideline compared to my other addictions.

Which of course brings up the business of so-called "process addictions," or "behavioral addictions" over the traditional substance addictions - with alcohol being the main one. This is where one is addicted to a behavioral repertoire, a behaviorlal programme, rather than something you put into your body. It's strange and somewhat difficult to understand for those who haven't gone through it - so much so that there's actually controversy in some circles as to whether it's a legitimate addiction or not!!! (Hard to believe as that may be).

But it totally existed for me, of course.

However, process addictions are so weird that even an approach to addiction recovery and support like Lifering Secular Recovery seems to have trouble addressing it directly - which, to me, is it's one major drawback. Nowhere in the Lifering literature do they seem to address the non-substance addictions... it almost makes me feel like we don't exist. Not that this makes me want to embrace 12-step approaches, but at least they are pretty open and embracing of those of us addicted to sexual stuff, gambling (also food, to name another process addiction). Regardless, despite that drawback, Lifering has been a good program for me - I've made it work. Maybe at some point I'll talk more about that.

Anyways, that's my submission for the day. Would like to hear some more about you.
